steps.text:
Because the paradigm is shifting from cloud to edge computing, deep learning models are now executed on devices that are low-power and tight on memory. Among the many models, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have become one of the most powerful tools for different tasks, including image recognition, and natural language and signal processing. However, running them efficiently on edge devices with limited resources is still a big challenge, because they have a high memory footprint and a huge number of operations. Various architectures have been proposed to deal with this challenge. ASICs give the highest performance and energy efficiency for specific applications because their hardware design is custom-tailored. In this work we look at Coarse-Grain Reconfigurable Arrays (CGRAs) for executing CNN applications, as possible candidates to cover a different part of the design space of edge computing systems (i.e., considering trade-offs between performance, energy efficiency, area and versatility).

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Because the paradigm is shifting from cloud to edge computing, deep learning models are now executed on devices that are low-power and tight on memory. Among the many models, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have become one of the most powerful tools for different tasks, including image recognition, and natural language and signal processing. However, running them efficiently on edge devices with limited resources is still a big challenge, because they have a high memory footprint and a huge number of operations. Various architectures have been proposed to deal with this challenge. ASICs give the highest performance and energy efficiency for specific applications because their hardware design is custom-tailored. FPGAs instead give more flexibility with their fine-grained reconfigurable architecture, so they are more versatile than ASICs, but they are generally less energy efficient. In this work we look at Coarse-Grain Reconfigurable Arrays (CGRAs) for executing CNN applications, as possible candidates to cover a different part of the design space of edge computing systems (i.e., considering trade-offs between performance, energy efficiency, area and versatility). CGRAs have programmable hardware that can be customized for specific tasks, so they are well-suited for dynamic edge computing environments. So they are an attractive meet-in-the-middle solution between performance, efficiency, and task-versatility. But to exploit their potential benefits, the convolutional layers have to be mapped onto CGRAs efficiently. Figure 1 shows an example of how a convolution is mapped on our target CGRA.

Several works have looked at mapping techniques for high performance CGRAs or at specializing CGRAs for deep learning, but low-power (mW -power), general-purpose CGRAs have not been explored as much for tinyML. To fill this gap, in this work we address the problem of mapping convolutions, and we focus on the OpenEdgeCGRA architecture for edge computing applications. Our goal is to outline efficient practices that make it possible to leverage this accelerator while minimizing the impact of the overheads it imposes. For this we investigate various state-of-the-art computational and memory management strategies, with the aim of finding the most efficient mapping technique that balances performance and resource constraints. Our contribution is two-fold: (i) we explore different implementation paradigms for convolution and different tensor parallelism axes; (ii) we benchmark the results of the different implementations, measuring energy, latency, performance, and memory usage, and we give insights on the best mapping technique for low-power CGRA. This analysis shows that direct convolution together with weight parallelism is the best, reaching up to 3.4\times in energy and 9.9\times in latency compared to a plain CPU implementation, and achieving an overall average performance of 0.6\nicefrac{{MAC}}{{cycle}}.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The shift from cloud to edge computing has led to executing deep learning models on low-power and memory-tight devices. Among the many models, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have emerged as one of the most powerful tools for various tasks, including image recognition, and natural language and signal processing. However, executing them efficiently on resource-constrained edge devices remains a significant challenge, given their high memory footprint and huge number of operations. To cope with this challenge, various architectures have been proposed. ASICs offer the highest performance and energy efficiency for specific applications thanks to their custom-tailored hardware design [1]. FPGAs, on the other hand, provide more flexibility through their fine-grained reconfigurable architecture, making them more versatile than ASICs but generally less energy efficient [2]. In this work, we explore Coarse-Grain Reconfigurable Arrays (CGRAs) as potential candidates to cover a different part of the design space of edge computing systems (i.e., considering trade-offs between performance, energy efficiency, area and versatility) for executing CNN applications [3]. CGRAs present programmable hardware that can be customized to specific tasks, which makes them well-suited for dynamic edge computing environments. Thus, they offer an attractive meet-in-the-middle solution between performance, efficiency, and task-versatility. Nevertheless, efficiently mapping convolutional layers onto CGRAs is essential to exploit their potential benefits. Figure 1 shows an example of mapping a convolution on our target CGRA.

Although several works have focused on mapping techniques for high performance CGRAs [4] or on specializing CGRAs for deep learning [3,5], low-power (mW -power), general-purpose CGRAs have not been explored to the same extent for tinyML [6]. To fill this gap, this work addresses the problem of mapping convolutions, focusing on the OpenEdgeCGRA architecture for edge computing applications [7]. Our goal is to outline efficient practices that allow this accelerator to be leveraged while minimizing the impact of the overheads it imposes. To this end, we investigate various state-of-the-art computational and memory management strategies, aiming to find the most efficient mapping technique that balances performance and resource constraints. Specifically, we present a two-fold contribution: (i) we explore different implementation paradigms for convolution and different tensor parallelism axes; (ii) we benchmark the different implementations, measuring energy, latency, performance, and memory usage, and provide insights on the best mapping technique for low-power CGRA. This analysis highlights the predominance of direct convolution combined with weight parallelism, which reaches up to 3.4\times and 9.9\times in terms of energy and latency, respectively, compared to a plain CPU implementation, with an overall average performance of 0.6\nicefrac{{MAC}}{{cycle}}.

References:
[1] Norman P Jouppi et al. In-datacenter performance analysis of a tensor processing unit. In Proc. of the 44th ISCA , pages 1–12, 2017.
[2] Yixing Li et al. A gpu-outperforming fpga accelerator architecture for binary convolutional neural networks. ACM JETC , 14:1 – 16, 2017.
[3] Jungi Lee and Jongeun Lee. Specializing cgras for light-weight convolutional neural networks. IEEE TCAD , 41(10):3387–3399, 2021.
[4] Dhananjaya Wijerathne et al. Himap: Fast and scalable high-quality mapping on cgra via hierarchical abstraction. IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems , 41(10):3290–3303, 2021.
[5] Christian Heidorn et al. Design space exploration for layer-parallel execution of convolutional neural networks on cgras. In Proc. of the 23th SCOPES , pages 26–31, 2020.
[6] Artur Podobas et al. A survey on coarse-grained reconfigurable architectures from a performance perspective. IEEE Access , 8:146719–146743, 2020.
[7] Rubén Rodríguez Álvarez et al. An open-hardware coarse-grained reconfigurable array for edge computing. In Proc. of the 20th ACM CF , pages 391–392, 2023.
